title: How Trump's H-1B Visa Overhaul Is Fueling India's Startup Boom
excerpt: A $100,000 visa fee, plunging student arrivals, and a maturing startup ecosystem are reversing the decades-old brain drain from India to the United States.
body:
• Trump's $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa applications has made it commercially unviable for many US companies to hire from India, according to analysts at Crisil and Jefferies.
  • Recruitment firms report a five-fold increase in US-based Indian tech talent exploring job opportunities back in India.
  • India's startup ecosystem has grown from 50,000 recognized startups in 2020 to over 200,000 today, with deep-tech ventures leading a funding rebound.
  • IIT directors say the country's brightest engineers no longer see US jobs as essential, with global capability centers offering high-end roles at home.

When Kunal Bahl's H-1B visa application was rejected in 2007, the India-born Wharton MBA packed his bags and left Microsoft for home. "My heart sank when I got word," he told Bloomberg Businessweek. "Such decisions are one-sided and irreversible." Nearly two decades later, Bahl's involuntary return looks less like a setback and more like a preview of what is now becoming a structural shift in Indian tech talent flows.

President Donald Trump's imposition of a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa applications has upended the economics of hiring Indian workers in the United States. Rating agency Crisil estimates the change could add $150 million to $550 million in annual costs for top Indian IT companies, while brokerage Jefferies warns profits could shrink by as much as 1.5 percent per H-1B worker, according to Livemint.

A Five-Fold Surge in Returnee Interest

"We're seeing nearly a five-fold increase in US-based talent actively exploring opportunities across India," Anshul Lodha, managing director at recruitment firm PageGroup India, told Livemint. "Fintech, banks, consumer tech, conglomerates, and PE/VC funds are increasingly open to hiring US-trained talent."

The shift extends to education. Indian student arrivals in the United States plunged 44.5 percent in August 2025 — the steepest drop since the pandemic, according to Livemint. Applications from Indian students to US colleges have fallen 14 percent since Trump's return to the White House, according to Common App data reported by Bloomberg News.

"We're not seeing US H-1B tightening as a setback. It's a signal for a structural shift."

— Kunal Singhal, Founder, Eazy Business Solutions

India's Startup Ecosystem Steps Up

India's startup landscape has matured rapidly. Recognized startups have grown from roughly 50,000 in 2020 to more than 200,000 today, according to figures from the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, placing India among the world's top three startup hubs. Deep-tech startups have raised $1.06 billion through July 2025 — double the previous year's pace — and the government's second ₹10,000 crore Startup Fund tranche is focused entirely on deep-tech, Livemint reported.

At the same time, global capability centers (GCCs) operated by companies such as Microsoft, Amazon, JPMorgan Chase, and Goldman Sachs have expanded across Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Pune. Bloomberg News reported that these hubs now handle critical, high-end work — so vital that one European bank concluded a major disruption in India would hit its global activities more than a similar disaster at its headquarters.

IITs See Opportunity, Not Crisis

"It's possibly an opportunity for some of us," Rangan Banerjee, director of IIT-Delhi, told Bloomberg News. "We want our students to be job creators." At IIT Bombay, domestic job offers outnumbered international ones even before the immigration clampdown: in the 2023-24 academic year, just 78 of 1,475 accepted offers came from international companies.

Ashok Jhunjhunwala, founder of the IIT-Madras Research Park, told Bloomberg: "There is a tremendous raw talent in India." Akshay Sharma, a 19-year-old IIT-Delhi student, captured the generational shift: "Last year, I would not have thought to do this," he said of seeking internships in both India and the US.

The Challenges of Coming Home

Returnees face real trade-offs. Professionals can expect salary adjustments of 25 to 50 percent, according to PageGroup. "Dollar to rupee conversion doesn't make sense," said Selva S., a semiconductor engineer who returned after 17 years in the US. "Getting 40 percent of the US salary in India is decent."

India's cloud, chip, and AI compute infrastructure also lags behind the US. "Only when India creates an environment comparable to the US — in infrastructure, innovation, and opportunity — will talent truly stay," said Aadesh Goyal, former CHRO of Tata Communications. Mohandas Pai, former Infosys CFO, argued the bottleneck is capital, not talent: "With capital, you can hire talent from anywhere."

What's Next

The real test is whether India can absorb its returning talent and give it reason to stay. By 2035, more than half of India's startups could emerge from tier-II and tier-III cities, potentially creating 50 million jobs and lifting the startup sector's share of GDP from 4-5 percent to nearly 15 percent, according to a report from the Indus Entrepreneurs (TiE). For the Indian diaspora watching from the US, the calculus has changed: the American dream now comes with a $100,000 surcharge, and the Indian alternative is no longer a consolation prize.
